planting.note: Divide established clumps of this naturally occurring white-flowered form in early fall or early spring rather than growing from seed, since seedlings often revert toward the species' typical pink-lilac color; plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing clumps 12-18 inches apart. This naturally occurring white-flowered form of wild geranium was first documented in the Great Smoky Mountains and is otherwise identical to the species, producing the same deeply lobed foliage and April-to-June bloom window, but with pure white rather than pink-lilac petals. Because the white color does not always come true from seed, propagate named stock by division to maintain the trait reliably. Combine with spring ephemerals in a woodland border for a cooling contrast against the far more common pink-flowered form.

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine, dust-like seed in spring without covering, since it needs light to germinate; this seed-propagated strain, selected by Dale Hendricks from wild North Carolina mountain populations, produces variable but consistently attractive silver-marbled foliage.

directions: Grow in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to light woodland shade, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart. Dale's Strain is a seed-propagated selection of native American alumroot chosen for its variable foliage, which typically emerges chartreuse with olive mottling and matures to silvery-green with contrasting spruce-green veins before turning gold-orange in fall. Tiny pinkish-white bell flowers rise on wiry stems in late spring, but the mottled evergreen foliage is the main attraction. Because it tolerates dry shade and root competition better than most Heuchera selections, it performs especially well as a groundcover under established trees where irrigation is limited.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to full shade; a selection of native Heuchera villosa chosen for its large, glossy, sycamore-shaped bronze-red foliage and rigid, statuesque habit.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to full shade, spacing clumps 15-24 inches apart to allow the large foliage mound room to develop. Bronze Wave was one of ten top performers out of 83 cultivars evaluated in Mount Cuba Center's multi-year Heuchera trial, prized for its thick, glossy, lacquer-like bronze-red leaves shaped like small sycamore leaves and its vigorous, uniform habit. Small whitish flowers appear on tall wiry stems in late summer and early fall, later than most coral bells, extending the bloom season for pollinators. As a straight selection of the native southeastern species Heuchera villosa, it tolerates summer heat, humidity, and dry shade with tree-root competition better than many complex hybrid coral bells.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in early fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade to part sun; tolerates more direct sun than most woodland phlox provided soil stays consistently moist.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light woodland shade to part sun, spacing plants 12-15 inches apart. Native to open montane woodlands, woodland borders, and rocky barrens of the central Appalachians from Pennsylvania to North Carolina and Tennessee, mountain phlox forms a low, creeping mat of basal foliage from which upright flowering stems rise in late spring, topped with fragrant pink flower clusters. It is more tolerant of sun and average garden moisture than the closely related woodland phlox (Phlox divaricata), making it a useful choice for the brighter edges of a shade garden. Deadhead spent flower clusters to keep the low foliage mat tidy through summer.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in constantly moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; native to Appalachian seepages, spray cliffs, and brookbanks and needs steady moisture at the root zone to thrive.

directions: Plant in constantly moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart near a shaded seep, streambank, or drainage where soil never fully dries out. Native to the Appalachian mountains of Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, and North Carolina, mountain meadow-rue grows naturally in wooded seepages and beside cold mountain streams and waterfalls, producing airy, blue-green, finely divided foliage reminiscent of a small columbine. Loose, open clusters of small white flowers with prominent stamens appear from May through July, held well above the delicate foliage on wiry stems. It is an excellent choice for the wet, shaded edge of a rain garden or streamside planting where few other woodland wildflowers will tolerate the constant moisture.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; closely resembles Canada wild ginger but is distinguished by its sharply reflexed calyx lobes and its more easterly-to-Ozark distribution.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil with a circumneutral pH in partial to full shade, spacing new divisions 9-12 inches apart. Reflexed wild ginger was long treated as a variety of the more familiar Canada wild ginger but is now recognized as a distinct species, ranging from Connecticut west to Manitoba and south to the Carolinas, Arkansas, and Oklahoma in rich deciduous forest. It forms a low, spreading carpet of paired, heart-shaped, matte green leaves that hide small maroon, jug-shaped flowers at ground level in early spring. Use it exactly as you would Canada wild ginger, as a slow-spreading, deer-resistant groundcover for dense shade beneath mature deciduous trees.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Scatter seed on moist prepared soil in fall, pressing lightly onto the surface, or transplant nursery divisions in spring; naturalizes readily in woodland soil and tolerates heavier, patchier moisture than many other native violets.

directions: Plant in well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants 6-12 inches apart; Missouri violet tolerates heavier soil, patchy moisture, and light foot traffic better than most stemless blue violets. Native from Minnesota and Ontario south to Georgia and west to New Mexico, it is distinguished from the closely related common blue violet by its longer, triangular, heart-shaped leaves and paler lilac flowers marked with a darker eyespot around the throat. It colonizes by rhizome to form a loose, low groundcover in open woodland and along woodland edges, blooming in early spring. As with other native violets, it serves as a larval host plant for several fritillary butterfly species and an early nectar source for native bees.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in humus-rich, moist to dry-mesic soil in partial to full shade; restricted to beech-dominated slopes of the Ozark and Ouachita mountains and a species of conservation concern, so purchase only nursery-propagated stock.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in humus-rich, moist to dry-mesic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 6-10 inches apart. Ozark wakerobin is a regional variety of dwarf trillium restricted to beech-dominated dry to dry-mesic slopes of the Ozark and Ouachita mountains of Arkansas and Missouri, distinguished from the eastern Coastal Plain form by its drier upland habitat and narrower leaves. A single small, erect, white flower with slightly rolled green sepals opens atop a short stalk in April and May before fading to pink with age. Because wild populations are of regional conservation concern, plant only propagated stock and site it in an undisturbed woodland garden away from foot traffic.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil on rocky slopes or ledges in partial to full shade; differs from the typical form mainly in its more densely hairy leaves and stems, an adaptation associated with its higher-elevation Appalachian range.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil on rocky slopes, ledges, or wooded banks in partial to full shade, spacing clumps 12-18 inches apart. This variety of American alumroot occurs on rock outcrops and wooded bluffs of the central and southern Appalachians, where it is distinguished from the typical form by its more densely hairy leaves and flowering stems. Like the species, it forms a mounded clump of rounded, marbled foliage with wiry stems of small greenish-white flowers in late spring, and it shares the species' tolerance for shallow, rocky, seasonally dry soil. Use it on shaded rock gardens, retaining walls, or slopes where its hairy texture and adaptability to thin soil are assets.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; long included within Canada wild ginger but now recognized as a distinct species of the north-central and east-central United States.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing new divisions 9-12 inches apart beneath deciduous trees. Hydra ginger is a long-lived rhizomatous woodland species of rich deciduous forests in the north-central and east-central United States, previously classified as a variety of Canada wild ginger and separated primarily by its pointed leaf tips and flower structure. Its paired, broadly heart-shaped leaves arise directly from a spreading rhizome and hide small, jug-shaped maroon flowers at ground level in early spring. Grow it as a slow, dense, deer-resistant groundcover under the same conditions used for Canada wild ginger.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
